sentences: There is a persistent misunderstanding about doubt and uncertainty in science, which fuels a significant amount of contemporary distrust towards it.
Many confuse uncertainty with ignorance and conclude that if scientists are "not sure," it means they don't know, and that their word is therefore no better than anyone else's.
This reasoning is based on a profound misconception.
For acknowledging uncertainty is not admitting ignorance; on the contrary, it is a sophisticated form of knowledge, one that understands the limits of what it asserts.
First, we must distinguish two meanings of the word "uncertainty."
There is the uncertainty of someone who knows nothing, who has no idea, who is completely in the dark: that is ignorance.

And there is the uncertainty of someone who knows a lot but precisely understands the extent of what they do not know, who can say not only what they consider established, but also with what degree of confidence, and where the gray areas begin.
This second uncertainty is not the opposite of knowledge; it is an advanced component of it.
The scholar who says, "we know this with great confidence, that with less, and we still do not know this" knows infinitely more than someone who asserts everything with equal assurance.
This measured uncertainty is even characteristic of a rigorous scientific approach.
Science does not operate on absolute certainties, but on degrees of confidence, constantly adjusted as evidence accumulates.
A scientific assertion is always accompanied, implicitly or explicitly, by an evaluation of its solidity: is it solidly established, probable, hypothetical?
This gradation is not a weakness; it is honesty and precision.
Where ideology or belief assert everything with the same confidence, science distinguishes what it knows from what it assumes, and this distinction is a superiority, not a flaw.
That is why it is misleading, and often dishonest, to exploit scientific uncertainty to disqualify what science establishes.

"Scientists do not agree," "it's just a theory," "nothing is certain": these phrases play on the confusion between the uncertainty that accompanies all rigorous knowledge and the absence of knowledge.
The fact that a theory has areas of uncertainty does not mean it is based on nothing; that a disagreement exists on fine points does not mean that the essentials are in debate.
Using the existence of a margin of uncertainty to reject a solidly established knowledge is to cynically exploit the very integrity of science against itself.

This strategy has been deliberately employed, history shows, by those who had an interest in delaying action: fostering doubt, exaggerating uncertainty, presenting a solid consensus as an open controversy, in order to paralyze under the pretext that we "might not be sure."

This manufacturing of doubt precisely exploits our misunderstanding of scientific uncertainty: by presenting it as ignorance, it turns the virtue of science — its honesty about its limits — into an argument against it.
There is no more effective defense of inaction than to demand an absolute certainty that no science can ever provide.
Understanding that doubt is not ignorance is therefore a way to guard against this manipulation.

It is to recognize that knowledge which knows its limits is better than blind certainty, that measured uncertainty is a form of rigor, and that demanding total certainty before acting is often a disguised way of refusing to act.
Science does not offer us absolute certainties, because it is honest; but it offers us the best available knowledge, along with an indication of its reliability.

Turning away from it on the grounds that it is not absolutely certain is to prefer the illusion of certainty over the reality of knowledge — and to condemn oneself, in the name of a misunderstood doubt, to being unable to believe or decide anything.

sentences: Technological progress often manifests itself as convenience: everything becomes easier, faster, and less burdensome.
What used to require effort, time, and hardship can now be done effortlessly, in an instant, without difficulty.
This promise of convenience is so obviously desirable that we hardly think to question it: who would want difficulty when ease is available?
And yet, we must dare to ask whether convenience, this seemingly flawless good, has a hidden cost, and whether everything that spares us effort truly serves us.
Let's start by acknowledging what is legitimate about convenience.
Many of the efforts that technology spares us were pure burdens, without value, and being freed from them is an undeniable progress.
No one sincerely regrets washing their clothes by hand, traveling miles for information, or painstakingly copying texts.
These hardships had no virtue; freeing ourselves from them has opened up time and energy for better things.
In these cases, convenience is a pure blessing, and denying it would be an absurd form of dolorism that confuses effort with value.
But not all efforts are mere burdens, and this is where convenience becomes ambiguous.
For some efforts have value, not despite their difficulty, but because of it.

The effort to learn builds skills; the effort to search leads to encounters with what we weren't looking for; the effort to do things ourselves provides a competence and satisfaction that the result obtained without effort does not.
When convenience spares us those efforts, it does not just serve us: it also deprives us of what effort produced.
We gain time, but we lose what the time spent brought us.
There is something more subtle.
Widespread convenience gradually makes us incapable of effort by atrophying the skills it spares us from exercising.
By getting everything effortlessly, we lose the habit and taste for effort, until the slightest obstacle seems unbearable.
Ease creates a need for ease, an increasing intolerance for anything that resists, and impatience for anything that does not come immediately.

Thus, convenience, by sparing us effort, makes us unfit for effort, and this unfitness has a cost, because many precious things — mastery, depth, perseverance — require precisely what convenience teaches us to unlearn.
That's not all.
Convenience also has a price that we do not see because it is paid elsewhere.
What is made so easy for us often relies on invisible labor, consumed resources, and costs shifted to others or to the future.
Instant delivery, immediate access, and permanent service assume entire chains of efforts and expenses that convenience hides from us.
We enjoy ease without seeing the price, which is very real, but paid out of our sight.
Convenience does not abolish effort and cost; it displaces them, makes them invisible, and shifts the burden onto others.
Recognizing the price of convenience does not mean rejecting it outright, nor advocating a return to difficulty as a virtue.

It means distinguishing between the efforts that are good to be freed from and those that were worth making, and asking ourselves, in front of each new convenience, what it spares us and what it costs us.
Sometimes it means deliberately choosing effort where it has value, preferring to do things ourselves, to search, to learn, rather than delegating everything to convenience.

In a world that elevates ease to the highest value, reserving spaces for chosen effort is not archaic; it is preserving what convenience, by sparing us too much, ultimately takes away: the ability to do, to struggle, to earn what we obtain.

sentences: The ecological crisis raises a new kind of moral question: do we have duties to future generations, to those who have not yet been born?
Our present actions — what we consume, destroy, and bequeath — will profoundly affect the world that those who come after us will inherit.
But these future people do not yet exist; they cannot ask us for anything, protest, or negotiate.
Can we have obligations to beings who do not exist, and if so, what are these obligations based on?
This question, seemingly abstract, governs our relationship with the future.
A first difficulty lies in the fact that future generations cannot claim any rights, since they do not exist.
We have duties, it is said, to those who have rights; but can a being that does not exist have rights?

This objection has logical force, but it clashes with a powerful intuition: it seems clear to us that bequeathing a devastated world to future generations would be a wrongdoing, that we do not have the right to enjoy the present while ruining their future.
This intuition withstands the logical objection and suggests that our duties to the future cannot be reduced to the logic of rights and claims.
So, on what basis can we found these duties?
We can first note that, while future people do not yet exist individually, it is certain that there will be future generations, and their fate depends on us.
We know that they will exist, that they will have needs, and that they will suffer or thrive depending on the world we leave for them.
This certainty may be enough to establish an obligation: not to a specific individual, but to those, whoever they may be, who will inherit our actions.

We are in the position of someone who sets a trap on a path where they know others will pass: it does not matter that they do not know who; they know that someone will suffer from their act, and that is enough to make them responsible.
We can also base these duties on the idea of continuity between generations, a chain of which we are merely one link.
We have received from our predecessors a world, knowledge, institutions, a heritage; we enjoy it without having created it.
This debt to the past calls for a symmetrical duty to the future: to pass on in turn, not to break the chain, not to squander a heritage that we only temporarily hold.
We are not absolute owners of the world, free to enjoy it until it is exhausted; we are its custodians, tasked with passing it on.
This conception, present in many traditions, grounds our duties to the future in our place within a continuity that transcends us.
The real difficulty may not be so much in establishing these duties as in feeling them.

For our obligations to the future encounter a major psychological obstacle: the distant future is abstract to us, future generations are foreign to us, and we spontaneously give much more weight to the present than to a future that will no longer concern us.
We know intellectually that we should care about the future, but we feel it poorly, and this lack of feeling paralyzes action.
The problem is not that we ignore our duties to the future, but that we struggle to feel them with enough strength to act accordingly.
Overcoming this obstacle is one of the great moral challenges of our time.

It is not enough to theoretically establish our duties to future generations; we must learn to feel them, to concretely care about a future we will not see, to expand our moral horizon beyond our own existence.
This requires a form of imagination and generosity: to care for those we will never know, to act for a world we will not enjoy, to plant trees under whose shade we will not sit.
This ability to care for the distant future is not natural; it is an achievement, almost a virtue.
But it is this virtue that may determine the fate of those who will succeed us — and the dignity of what we leave them.

sentences: It is easy to imagine that threats to democracy come from its declared enemies: tyrants, extremists, those who want to overthrow it.

We forget a more subtle, but perhaps equally serious threat: the apathy of citizens, this growing disinterest in public affairs, this abstention, this feeling that politics does not concern us or will not change anything.
For a democracy cannot survive without the participation of its citizens; their withdrawal empties it of its substance, hands it over to others, and allows it to wither away.
Apathy does not attack democracy head-on; it undermines it from within.
We must first understand the causes of this apathy, as it is not a simple laziness that can be blamed on citizens.

It often stems from a feeling of powerlessness: what’s the point of getting involved, voting, mobilizing, if one feels that nothing changes, that decisions are made elsewhere, that our voice carries no weight?

This feeling is not unfounded: the increasing complexity of issues, the distance between citizens and decision-making places, the weight of forces that escape voting, can create the impression that democratic participation is futile.
Apathy is often less about indifference than about discouragement, the result of a feeling of powerlessness.
It also arises from disappointment.
Many citizens have turned away from politics after being let down by it: unfulfilled promises, corruption, the feeling that those in power serve their own interests rather than the common good.
This disappointment breeds a distrust that turns into withdrawal: since we cannot trust them, what’s the point of getting involved?
Apathy is then the consequence of a loss of trust in those in power and institutions, a disengagement out of frustration.
It is not the primary cause of the problem, but its symptom: it reflects a crisis in the relationship between citizens and their democracy.
However, regardless of its causes, apathy has serious consequences for democracy.
First, it deprives democracy of the participation on which it relies: a democracy where citizens no longer engage is nothing more than a shell, an electoral ritual stripped of meaning.
Next, it leaves the field open to those who remain mobilized: organized interests, active minorities, those who have the means to exert influence.
When the majority withdraws, it is not a void that prevails, but the power of those who do not withdraw; the apathy of some empowers others.

Finally, it weakens democracy in the face of its enemies: an disengaged, disillusioned, indifferent people is fertile ground for those who would like to replace it with other regimes, as they will not defend what no longer interests them.
There is a vicious circle here that must be named.

Powerlessness and disappointment lead to apathy; apathy weakens democracy and hands power to special interests; this weakening increases the feeling of powerlessness and disappointment, which in turn feeds apathy.
How can we break this circle?

Not by blaming disengaged citizens, which would only worsen their distrust, but by restoring what has been lost: the feeling that participation matters, that citizens' voices count, that politics can change things.
This requires institutions that return power to citizens, a political life that deserves trust, leaders who serve the common good rather than betray it.
Thus, fighting against apathy is not just a matter of individual civic duty, but of a collective restoration of the meaning of democracy.
Everyone can, of course, refuse to be discouraged, engage nonetheless, exercise their share of citizenship; and this individual commitment has its value.
But apathy will only dissipate sustainably if democracy gives its citizens reasons to believe that their participation matters.
For one only engages if one thinks it can change something, and massive disengagement is primarily a sign that too many citizens have stopped believing this.
Restoring democracy's ability to change things is the only lasting remedy to the apathy that threatens it.

sentences: We consider metaphor to be an ornament of discourse, a figure of style used in poetry, a deviation from literal language that would express things directly.
This conception, inherited from a long tradition, makes metaphor an accessory, an expressive luxury that one could, if necessary, do without.
However, this may be profoundly false.

For it could be that metaphor, far from being an occasional ornament, structures our thinking entirely, that we think in metaphors without realizing it, and that supposedly literal language is itself filled with forgotten metaphors.
This hypothesis, which contemporary reflection has explored, overturns our relationship with language and thought.
Let’s observe our most ordinary language, the one we believe to be literal.

We say that our arguments are solid or that they collapse, that we grasp an idea or that it escapes us, that time passes, that prices rise, that we are at the peak of our form or at the bottom of despair.

These expressions, which we no longer perceive as figurative because they are so worn out, are nonetheless metaphors: they draw from the realm of the concrete, of space, of physical movement, to express the abstract, thought, and emotions.
We conceive of ideas as objects that can be grasped, arguments as structures that stand or collapse, time as a movement, and states of mind as positions in space.
These metaphors are so deeply embedded in our language that we no longer perceive them as such; they have become the very fabric of our thought.
This observation has considerable implications.
For if we think the abstract through the concrete, emotions through space, and ideas through objects, then our metaphors do not merely express our thoughts: they shape them.
The way we conceive of something depends on the metaphor through which we apprehend it.

Conceiving of discussion as a war — attacking a position, defending a point, winning or losing a debate — is not neutral: this war metaphor shapes our very way of discussing, making us see the interlocutor as an opponent to defeat rather than as a partner in the search for truth.
Changing the metaphor changes the thing: conceiving of discussion as a joint construction, a dance, an exploration, would transform our approach to it.
The metaphors through which we live are not just ways of speaking; they are ways of thinking, and thus of acting.
This discovery sheds light on entire aspects of our existence.
Our fundamental metaphors — about time, life, mind, and society — silently guide our understanding and our behavior.
To conceive of life as a journey, a struggle, a game, or a burden engages different attitudes; to conceive of the mind as a machine, a garden, or a container directs how we treat it.
These metaphors, which we did not choose, which we inherited from our language and culture, govern our thought without our awareness, like invisible presuppositions.
Becoming aware of their power is to gain freedom over them: the freedom to question them, to change them, to choose which metaphors we want to think and live by.
It is not about, in recognizing the omnipresence of metaphor, falling into the idea that everything is metaphor, that there is no literal language, no literal truth.
This excessive conclusion would dissolve the distinction between the true and the figurative, without which thought itself wavers.

There is indeed a more literal language, statements whose metaphorical value is null or negligible; but this literal language is narrower than one might have thought, and the abstract, in particular, is hardly expressed without metaphor.
Recognizing this does not deny all literalness; it measures how much metaphor, far from being an ornament that the abstract could do without, is often the only access to it.
The power of metaphors thus teaches us a lesson in humility and vigilance.

In humility, because we discover that our thought, which we believed to be self-mastering, is permeated with metaphors that guide it without our awareness, inherited from a language and culture that think within us before we think.

In vigilance, because recognizing this power invites us to examine the metaphors through which we live, to unearth those that mislead us, to choose, as much as possible, the figures that illuminate rather than those that obscure.

For we cannot think without metaphors; but we can, by becoming aware of their power, stop being their playthings and become, a little, their masters — and discover that changing the way we express things is already beginning to change the way we live them.

sentences: Our era measures value by success.
Those who succeed, who prevail, who win are considered great; those who fail, who lose, who are defeated are deemed contemptible, or at least negligible.
This identification of value with success is so deeply ingrained that it seems obvious.

And yet, a contrary intuition, ancient and persistent, endures: that there are defeats greater than victories, a greatness of the defeated that is not found in success, and that the value of a life is not measured by its triumph.
This intuition deserves to be explored, as it touches on what gives life its worth.
History and human memory preserve, alongside the victors, the traces of the defeated whose defeat was greater than many victories.

Those who fought for a just cause and lost, who resisted oppression and were crushed, who defended a value until death without triumphing, possess a greatness that their defeat does not erase, and which it sometimes even enhances.

We venerate certain defeated individuals more than many victors, not despite their defeat, but through it; for their defeat testifies to a loyalty to what is worth more than success, a refusal to sacrifice the essential for victory.
There is a greatness that reveals itself precisely in failure, when failure is the price of loyalty.
Let us understand what constitutes this greatness of the defeated.
It lies in the fact that the value of what they fought for does not depend on its success.
A just cause does not become unjust because it is defeated; a loyalty does not lose its worth because it fails; a fight for what is valuable retains its nobility even when lost.

He who subordinates everything to victory, who betrays his values to win, may win, but he loses the essential; he who remains faithful to what is valuable, even at the cost of defeat, may lose, but he saves the essential.

The greatness of the defeated is that of those who preferred to lose while remaining faithful rather than to win by betraying; it testifies that certain things are worth more than success, and that remaining faithful to them, even when defeated, is a victory of a different kind.
This greatness illuminates a truth that the cult of success obscures: the value of a life is not measured by its success.

A life can be a failure in the eyes of the world — without glory, without triumph, without success — and yet be great, if it has been faithful to what is valuable, if it has served a just cause, if it has refused to betray the essential.
Conversely, a life crowned with success can be mediocre, even vile, if that success was purchased at the cost of betraying everything that matters.
Success is not the measure of value; it can coexist with baseness, just as greatness can coexist with failure.
What gives a life its worth is what it has been faithful to, not what it has obtained.
This recognition of the greatness of the defeated has a comforting and liberating significance.

Comforting, because it frees us from the tyranny of success, from the anxiety of achieving, from the shame of failure; it tells us that our worth does not depend on our success, that we can fail and remain dignified, lose and still be great.
Liberating, because it allows us to place our loyalty elsewhere than in victory, to serve what is valuable without subordinating everything to success, to prefer justice to achievement.
He who has understood the greatness of the defeated is free with respect to success; he can seek it, but without sacrificing the essential, without making it the measure of his worth.
In celebrating the greatness of the defeated, it is not about praising failure, nor despising success, nor finding false comfort in one's defeats.
Not all defeats are great; there are failures that testify only to weakness or fault, and the greatness of the defeated belongs only to those whose defeat was the price of loyalty.

But recognizing this greatness means rejecting the identification of value with success, affirming that certain things are worth more than victory, and that remaining faithful to them, even when defeated, is the highest form of success.

In a world that only adores victors, remembering the greatness of the defeated preserves an essential truth: that the worth of a life is not measured by what it gains, but by what it remains faithful to.

sentences: Why does beauty move us?
Why do certain forms, certain sounds, certain spectacles evoke in us this particular emotion, this thrill, this pleasure sometimes mixed with tears, which we call aesthetic emotion?
This question, which seems simple, is actually one of the deepest and most enduring there is.
For none of the explanations given seem to fully exhaust it; there remains, in our emotion in the face of beauty, something that escapes, a mystery that reflection approaches without dispelling.
At the end of this meditation on beauty, it is worth pausing on this enigma, not to solve it, but to measure its depth.
Attempts have been made to explain aesthetic emotion in various ways.
Some have seen it as the recognition of harmony, proportion, or order that would meet a requirement of our mind; we would be moved by what presents formal perfection, a satisfying agreement of parts.

This explanation captures something, but it leaves something out: for not all beauty is harmony and proportion, and some beauties move us through their strangeness, their rupture, their excess, rather than through their order.
Harmony explains part of our emotion, but not its entirety or its mystery.
Others have sought the explanation in our nature, in our evolution, seeing it as an inherited disposition, a mechanism shaped by our history.
We would be moved by certain forms because this emotion would have had a function for our ancestors: to attract us to what is favorable, to divert us from what is harmful.
This approach has its fertility, it sheds light on some of our preferences; but it too leaves a considerable remainder.

For aesthetic emotion far exceeds what a simple adaptive function would explain; it pertains to objects — a work of art, a complex melody, a beautiful thought — that have no relation to our ancestors' survival.
The explanation by nature sheds light on the origin of certain dispositions, but not on the richness and depth of aesthetic emotion.
Others have linked aesthetic emotion to a meaning, to a significance, to what beauty tells or reveals to us.
We would be moved not by the form alone, but by what it expresses, by the truth it reveals, by the meaning it carries.
This approach is profound, and it accounts for the spiritual dimension of aesthetic emotion, for what it has beyond mere sensory pleasure.
But it too encounters a limit: for some beauties move us without us being able to say what they mean, by their mere sensible presence, independently of any formulable meaning.
Emotion often precedes and overflows any significance we might attach to it.
What strikes one in these attempts at explanation is that none exhausts the phenomenon, that all leave something out, that aesthetic emotion always seems to exceed what is said about it.
Perhaps this is the essence: that beauty, and the emotion it evokes, touch on something that resists explanation, that cannot be reduced to a cause, a function, or a meaning.
Aesthetic emotion puts us in the presence of something that transcends us, that exceeds our categories, that retains a part of mystery.

And it could be that this mystery is not a temporary limit of our knowledge, a riddle that one day will be solved, but an essential dimension of the phenomenon: that beauty is precisely what moves us without us being able to fully say why, what exceeds all explanation.

Recognizing this mystery is not giving up on understanding, nor sinking into the irrational; it is acknowledging the limits of explanation in the face of certain phenomena, and respecting what, in our experience, resists reduction.

The emotion in the face of beauty is one of those experiences that remind us that not everything can be explained, that our relationship with the world involves dimensions that exceed knowledge, that we are beings capable of being moved by what we do not fully understand.

And perhaps this is part of the value of beauty: that it opens us to a mystery, that it puts us in the presence of what transcends us, that it reminds us that human existence cannot be reduced to what can be explained and mastered.

Beauty moves us, and the fact that we do not quite know why is not a failure of our understanding, but perhaps a sign that we are touching, in this emotion, something essential that exceeds understanding itself.

sentences: We have distinguished between suffered solitude, which is suffering, and chosen solitude, which is richness.
But there is a third solitude, deeper than the other two, that no choice or company can abolish: essential solitude, which pertains to our very condition as conscious beings.
Each of us is a unique consciousness, a singular perspective on the world, confined in a sense to our own experience, which no one can fully share.

This solitude is neither a misfortune to be cured nor a good to be cultivated; it is a given of our condition that must be faced to understand what we are and what our relationships with others can or cannot be.
What does this essential solitude consist of?
It consists in the fact that each person experiences the world from their own point of view, in their own consciousness, and that this lived experience is, by nature, fundamentally incommunicable.
I cannot feel your pain as you feel it, nor can you feel mine; I cannot see the world through your eyes, nor enter your consciousness.
We can communicate, understand each other, draw closer; but there remains, at the core of each person, a lived experience that no one shares, a unique perspective that remains their own.

I am the only one who is me, the only one who feels what I feel from the inside; and this solitude, no company, no love, no communication can abolish, for it pertains to the very structure of consciousness.
This essential solitude reveals itself with particular acuity in certain experiences.
Suffering, first: the one who suffers is alone with their pain, which no one can feel in their place, however compassionate they may be.
Death, then, the ultimate trial of solitude: one dies alone, no one can die in our place nor accompany us beyond a certain threshold.
But also the most intimate experiences, the deepest thoughts, what is most personal in us, which remains, at its core, incommunicable.
There is in each person a core of solitude that nothing can break, a part of us that remains alone, regardless of our ties and surroundings.
This recognition may seem despairing, as if it condemns us to irredeemable isolation, as if others are forever inaccessible to us.
But that would be a misunderstanding of essential solitude.

For recognizing that there is in each person an incommunicable core does not mean that communication is impossible, that connections are futile, that we are locked in ourselves without access to others.
We communicate, we understand each other, we love each other, despite and through this solitude; simply, this communication does not abolish it entirely, it builds bridges over an abyss that remains.

Recognizing essential solitude does not deny the possibility of connection; it means understanding its true nature, which is not fusion but a meeting between beings who remain, at their core, distinct.
There is even something precious in this essential solitude when we understand it well.
For it is the correlate of our singularity, of our uniqueness, of what makes each person irreplaceable.

If we could completely merge into one another, fully share our experience, abolish all solitude, we would cease to be distinct individuals, unique consciousnesses; essential solitude is the price and the guarantee of our individuality.
It is what makes each person someone, a unique perspective on the world, a being who is not interchangeable.
Essential solitude is not just a limit to our relationships; it is also what underpins the value of each being as singular.
Understanding essential solitude transforms our relationship with others and with ourselves.
With ourselves, by reconciling with this part of irreducible solitude, by ceasing to experience it as a lack to be filled, by recognizing that it is the correlate of our singularity.

With others, by understanding that true connection is not the fusion that would abolish all distance, but the meeting that respects each person's solitude, the bridge thrown over the abyss that remains.
Loving others is not about abolishing their essential solitude or ours, but about recognizing and respecting that solitude while building bridges of love and understanding towards it.

The most beautiful relationship is not one that would deny essential solitude, but one that, recognizing it, unites two solitudes that respect each other — for, as a poet said, the highest love is perhaps that where two solitudes protect, limit, and greet each other.

sentences: Learning a foreign language, as we have seen, is not just about acquiring a tool for communication, a set of words and rules; it is about entering a world, a way of thinking, feeling, and experiencing.

This applies to all languages, but each language opens a particular world; and it is worth asking, at the end of this journey through the French language, what world, what sensitivity, and what way of being does learning French specifically open up.
For learning French is not just about gaining another language; it is about accessing a certain relationship with the world, of which it bears the trace.
Every language, as we have said, has lexicalized certain experiences, developed certain nuances, and favored certain relationships with the world.
French thus bears the mark of a certain sensitivity, a certain genius, shaped by a long history.

It has often been said that French is a language of clarity, precision, and rigor, made for analysis, distinction, and the exact expression of thought; a language that values order, structure, and clarity.

This reputation, like any generalization, must be nuanced; but it captures something of the genius of this language, its vocation for clear and distinct expression, and its appreciation for rigorous thinking.
French also bears the trace of a certain culture, a certain relationship to life, art, and thought.

Learning French means accessing a literature, a philosophy, and a tradition of thought that have marked the history of ideas; it means being able to read in their language works that have shaped our way of thinking; it means entering into a dialogue with a culture that has produced a significant part of what humanity has thought and created.

French is the language of a considerable intellectual and artistic tradition, and learning it gives you access to that tradition, not through the mediation of translation, but in the very language in which it was expressed.

But French is not just the language of France; it is spoken on several continents by diverse peoples who have made it their own, enriched it with their contributions, and turned it into the vehicle of their own cultures.
French is a language of sharing that connects different peoples, carries multiple cultures, and belongs not to a single nation but to all who speak it.
Learning French means accessing not just one world, but a plurality of worlds linked by a common language, a diversity of cultures that express themselves in the same language.
It is to enter a linguistic community that transcends the borders of a nation, uniting diverse peoples in the sharing of a language.

We must be careful, in celebrating the world that French opens up, not to fall into naive glorification, as if this language were superior to others, as if the world it opens were better than those opened by other languages.

Every language opens a world, and none is absolutely better than another; French is not superior, it is different, offering a particular access to a culture, a sensitivity, a tradition among others that are equally valuable.
Celebrating the world that French opens is not to regard it as the best, but to recognize that it opens, like any language, its own world, worthy of being known, which enriches those who access it.

At the end of this journey, someone who has learned French to the point of being able to read these demanding texts has thus gained more than just a language: they have gained a world, access to a culture, a sensitivity, a tradition; they have expanded their own world with a new one.

And this conquest is not just useful, an additional tool; it is an enrichment, an opening, a way to become broader, to multiply one's access to reality, no longer being a prisoner of a single way of seeing.

Learning French, like learning any language, is to give oneself an additional world; and those who possess multiple languages, multiple worlds, inhabit a richer, more diverse universe than those who know only one.

This is perhaps the most beautiful reward of this long learning process: not only being able to say and understand more, but having become, through the acquired language, a broader being, open to a world that, without it, would have remained closed to them.

sentences: Becoming oneself: this task, which seems the most natural, is in reality one of the most difficult there is, and it requires a courage that we underestimate.

For we are shaped by countless pressures — those of our environment, our education, the gaze of others, social expectations, and dominant models — that tend to make us conform, to turn us into what the world expects rather than what we truly are.
Becoming oneself, in this context, is not about following a natural slope; it is about resisting these pressures, conquering an existence that is truly one's own.
And this conquest demands a rare courage, the significance of which is worth measuring.
We have seen that the 'self' is not a given thing, a core that simply needs to be discovered, but something that is constructed.
Thus, becoming oneself is not about unearthing a hidden nature, but about making oneself, choosing oneself, constructing oneself, against what would shape us from the outside.
However, this construction of the self encounters powerful forces of conformity.
The desire to be accepted, to not displease, to belong, pushes us to conform, to embrace expectations, to silence what makes us unique.
The weight of others' gaze, the fear of disapproval, the pressure of the group, tends to make us fall in line, to erase what distinguishes us.
Becoming oneself means resisting these forces, daring to be different, and embracing one's uniqueness against the pressure to conform.
This courage to be oneself takes various forms.
It is the courage to have one's own opinions, to think for oneself, and not to adopt accepted ideas out of mere conformity.
It is the courage to make one's own choices, to follow one's path, and not to let one's existence be dictated by the expectations of others.
It is the courage to embrace one's uniqueness, what distinguishes us, what makes us different from others, instead of hiding it to fit in.
It is sometimes the courage to disappoint, to displease, to stray, when being true to oneself demands it.
All these forms share the commonality of resisting the pressure to conform, daring to be oneself against what would seek to make us conform.
This courage is rare because it is costly.
Conforming is easy, comfortable, and rewarded; one gains approval, belonging, and peace.
Being oneself, on the other hand, exposes one to disapproval, to the solitude of those who stray, and to the reproach of those who would like to see us similar to them.
The courage to be oneself must confront these costs, accept displeasing others, disappointing them, and sometimes finding oneself alone.
That is why so many people give it up, preferring the security of conformity to the discomfort of authenticity, the peace of conformity to the demand of being oneself.
Becoming oneself requires accepting these costs, preferring to be true to oneself rather than to be approved.
However, we must be careful not to misunderstand the courage to be oneself as merely a self-assertion against others, an individualism that would disdain others.
Being oneself is not about standing against others, nor about cultivating a superficial originality, nor about making one's difference a banner.
The true courage to be oneself is not ostentatious; it is often discreet, internal, and is more about quiet fidelity to what one believes and who one is than about spectacular rebellion.
It is not about distinguishing oneself for the sake of distinction, but about being true to oneself, which can very well coexist with respect for others and communal living.

The courage to be oneself is not the loud assertion of an ego against the world; it is the often silent fidelity to what one holds to be true and just, against the pressures that would lead us away from it.
This courage to be oneself is at the heart of wisdom, for there is no wise life that is not first a life that is truly one's own.
One cannot live wisely by living someone else's life, by adopting values that one has not made one's own, by conforming to what is expected of us.
Wisdom requires authenticity, fidelity to oneself, and the construction of an existence that is truly ours.
And this construction, against the pressures that shape us, demands this rare and discreet courage to be oneself, to think for oneself, to make one's own choices, and to embrace one's uniqueness.

Becoming oneself, against everything that would seek to conform us, is perhaps one of the most difficult and essential tasks of existence — and one of the conditions for a successful life that is coherent and true to its values, which we have said is the result of a life that has been shaped.

sentences: But despite all that, murmured Château-Renaud, Albert isn't coming; he's ten minutes late.
Here he is, said Beauchamp, he's on horseback; look, he's coming at full speed followed by his servant.
What recklessness, said Château-Renaud, to come on horseback to fight a duel!
I who had given him such a good lecture!
And then, look, said Beauchamp, with a collar on his tie, with an open coat, with a white waistcoat; why didn't he just have a fly drawn on his stomach right away?

It would have been simpler and over with sooner!” Meanwhile, Albert had arrived ten steps from the group formed by the five young men; he stopped his horse, jumped down, and handed the reins to his servant.
Albert approached.
He was pale, his eyes were red and swollen.
It was clear that he hadn't slept a second all night.
There was a shade of sad seriousness spread across his face that was unusual for him.
Thank you, gentlemen, he said, for having kindly responded to my invitation: believe me, I am extremely grateful to you for this gesture of friendship.
Goodbye!
Goodbye, our poor polar home!” said Mrs.
Paulina Barnett, waving her hand one last time.
And everyone, with this final memory, sadly and silently took the road back.
At one o'clock, the detachment had arrived at Cape Michel, after turning around the gap that the insufficient cold of winter had been unable to close.
Until then, the difficulties of the journey had not been great, as the ground of Victoria Island had a relatively flat surface.
But it would be quite different on the ice field.

Indeed, the icefield, subjected to the enormous pressure of the northern ice floes, had undoubtedly become rugged with icebergs, hummocks, and frozen mountains, among which they would have to search continuously for passable routes, at the cost of the greatest efforts and extreme fatigue.
By evening of that day, they had advanced a few miles onto the ice field.
They had to set up their sleeping arrangements.
To do this, they proceeded in the manner of the Eskimos and the Indians of North America, digging 'snow houses' in the ice blocks.

The snow knives worked effectively and skillfully, and at eight o'clock, after a dinner of dried meats, all the staff of the trading post had slipped into these holes, which are warmer than one might be tempted to believe.

sentences: Some of them, who had already arrived, were playing marbles on the stones of the cemetery.
Others, straddling the wall, were swinging their legs, cutting down the tall nettles that had grown between the low enclosure and the last graves.
It was the only place that was green; everything else was just stones, and constantly covered in a fine dust, despite the sacristan's broom.
The children in slippers ran around there as if on a floor made for them, and their voices could be heard ringing out through the buzzing of the bell.
It diminished with the swaying of the thick rope that, falling from the heights of the bell tower, dragged along the ground by its end.
Swallows flew by, letting out little cries, slicing through the air with the sharpness of their flight, and quickly returned to their yellow nests under the roof tiles.
At the back of the church, a lamp was burning, that is to say, a wick of a nightlight in a hanging glass.
From a distance, its light appeared as a whitish spot trembling on the oil.
A long ray of sunlight crossed the entire nave and made the aisles and corners even darker.
Where is the priest?
asked Madame Bovary of a young boy who was having fun shaking the turnstile in its too-loose hole.
Indeed, the door of the rectory creaked, and Abbé Bournisien appeared; the children, in a jumble, fled into the church.

And, picking up a tattered catechism that he had just bumped into with his foot, he stuffed the catechism into his pocket and stopped, continuing to swing the heavy key to the sacristy between two fingers.

sentences: The garden, longer than it was wide, stretched between two walls of rammed earth covered with espaliered apricots, all the way to a hedge of thorns that separated it from the fields.
In the middle, there was a slate sundial on a masonry pedestal; four flowerbeds filled with thin wild roses symmetrically surrounded the more practical square of serious vegetation.
At the very back, under the small fir trees, a plaster priest was reading his breviary.
Emma went up to the bedrooms.
The first one was unfurnished; but the second, which was the marital bedroom, had a mahogany bed in a recess with red drapery.
A shell box decorated the dresser; and on the writing desk, near the window, there was, in a carafe, a bouquet of orange blossoms tied with white satin ribbons.
It was a bridal bouquet, the bouquet from the other!
She looked at it.

Charles noticed this, took it, and went to put it in the attic, while Emma, sitting in an armchair (her belongings were arranged around her), thought about her wedding bouquet, which was packed in a box, and wondered, daydreaming, what would happen to it if she happened to die.
In the first few days, she occupied herself with contemplating changes in her house.

She removed the globes from the candlesticks, had new wallpaper put up, repainted the staircase, and had benches made in the garden all around the sundial; she even asked how to go about having a water fountain with fish.
Finally, her husband, knowing that she liked to go for drives, found a second-hand carriage that, with once new lanterns and studded leather mudguards, almost resembled a tilbury.

sentences: Having made this resolution, the next step was to carry it out.
It was only after long searches that Passepartout discovered a local antique dealer, to whom he presented his request.
The European outfit pleased the dealer, and soon Passepartout emerged dressed in an old Japanese robe and wearing a kind of ribbed turban, faded by the passage of time.
But in return, a few coins jingled in his pocket.

The first thing Passepartout did, now 'Japanese', was to enter a modest-looking tea house, where he had lunch made from leftover poultry and a few handfuls of rice, as a man for whom dinner would still be a problem to solve.
'Now,' he said to himself when he was well-fed, 'I must not lose my head.
I can no longer sell this rag for another one that is even more Japanese.
So I need to find a way to leave this land of the Sun as quickly as possible, of which I will only keep a lamentable memory!' Passepartout then thought about visiting the ships departing for America.
He planned to offer himself as a cook or servant, asking for nothing in return but passage and food.
Once in San Francisco, he would figure out how to get by.
The important thing was to cross the four thousand seven hundred miles of the Pacific that stretch between Japan and the New World.
Passepartout, being not the kind of man to let an idea linger, headed towards the port of Yokohama.
But as he approached the docks, his plan, which had seemed so simple when he first thought of it, appeared increasingly unfeasible.
Why would anyone need a cook or servant on an American liner, and what trust would he inspire, dressed like that?
What recommendations could he present?
What references could he provide?
I was called three months ago to the bedside of this old woman.
She had arrived the day before in the cart that served as her home, pulled by the nag you saw, and accompanied by her two large black dogs, her friends and guardians.
The priest was already there.
She made us her executors, and to reveal the meaning of her last wishes, she told us her whole life story.
I know nothing more singular and poignant.
Her father was a chair caner and her mother a chair caner as well.
She never had a home planted in the ground.
As a little girl, she wandered, ragged, verminous, and sordid.

They would stop at the entrance of villages, along the ditches; they would unhitch the cart; the horse would graze; the dog would sleep with its nose on its paws; and the little girl would roll in the grass while her parents repaired all the old seats of the community in the shade of the roadside elms.
They hardly spoke in that mobile home.
After a few necessary words to decide who would go around the houses shouting the well-known cry: 'Chair caner!', they would start twisting the straw, face to face or side by side.

When the child wandered too far or tried to make friends with some village urchin, her father's angry voice would call her back: 'Will you please come back here, you little rascal!' Those were the only words of tenderness she heard.
When she grew older, she was sent to collect the scraps of damaged seats.

Then she began to form some acquaintances here and there with the kids; but it was the parents of her new friends who would harshly call their children back: 'Will you please come here, you little scamp!'
'I want to see you talking to the ragamuffins!...'

sentences: The notary backed out while bowing deeply; it was the first time, since the day he had taken his registrations, that he encountered such a client.
As soon as the count was alone, he took a locked portfolio out of his pocket, which he opened with a small key attached to his neck that he never parted with.

After searching for a moment, he stopped at a sheet that had some notes, compared these notes with the sales document placed on the table, and, recalling his memories: "Auteuil, rue de la Fontaine, no. 28; that's it, he said; now should I rely on a confession extracted through religious terror or physical terror?
Besides, in an hour I will know everything.
Bertuccio!

he shouted, striking a kind of small folding-handle hammer on a bell that emitted a sharp and prolonged sound similar to that of a tam-tam, Bertuccio!" "Monsieur Bertuccio, said the count, didn't you once tell me that you had traveled in France?
--No, Excellence, no, replied the steward with a sort of nervous tremor that Monte-Cristo, an expert in emotions, rightly attributed to intense anxiety.

--It's unfortunate, he said, that you have never visited the surroundings of Paris, because I want to go see my new property this very evening, and by coming with me you would undoubtedly have given me useful information.
--To Auteuil?
exclaimed Bertuccio, whose coppery complexion turned almost ashen.
Me, go to Auteuil!
Well, what is so surprising about your coming to Auteuil, I ask you?
When I stay in Auteuil, you will have to come there, since you are part of the household.” Bertuccio lowered his head before the master's imperious gaze, and he remained motionless and silent.
Ah!
But what is happening to you?

Are you going to make me ring for the carriage a second time?” said Monte-Cristo in the tone that Louis XIV used to say the famous: “I could have waited!” Bertuccio only leaped from the small sitting room to the antechamber and shouted in a hoarse voice: Monte-Cristo wrote two or three letters; as he was sealing the last one, the steward reappeared.

sentences: As a child, young Vampa had a strange character.
One day, at the age of seven, he went to see the priest of Palestrina and asked him to teach him how to read.
It was a difficult task; for the young shepherd could not leave his flock.
But the good priest went every day to say mass in a poor little village too insignificant to pay a priest, and which, not even having a name, was known as dell'Borgo.
He offered Luigi to meet him on his way back and give him his lesson, warning him that this lesson would be short and that he should therefore make the most of it.

Every day, Luigi led his flock to graze along the road from Palestrina to the Borgo; every day, at nine in the morning, the priest would pass by, and the priest and the child would sit on the edge of a ditch, while the little shepherd took his lesson from the priest's breviary.

The priest had a writing teacher from Rome make three alphabets for him: one in large letters, one in medium, and one in small, and he showed him that by following this alphabet on a slate, he could learn to write with the help of a metal point.
The next day, he had gathered a supply of slates and set to work.
The priest, amazed by this profound intelligence and touched by this aptitude, gifted him several notebooks, a pack of pens, and a pocketknife.
It was a new study to undertake, but it was nothing compared to the first.
Eight days later, he handled the pen as skillfully as he handled the stylus.

The priest told this anecdote to the Count of San-Felice, who wanted to see the little shepherd, had him read and write in front of him, ordered his steward to have him eat with the servants, and gave him two piastres a month.
Indeed, he had applied this ease of imitation he possessed to all objects, and, like a young Giotto, he drew on his slates his sheep, trees, and houses.
Then, with the point of his pocketknife, he began to carve wood and give it all sorts of shapes.
This is how Pinelli, the popular sculptor, had started.

--I hold a grudge against him, replied Lord Wilmore, because when he was passing through England, he seduced the wife of one of my friends.
--But if you hold a grudge against him, why don't you seek revenge?
--I've already fought the count three times, said the Englishman: the first time with a pistol; the second time with a sword; the third time with a sabre.

--The first time, he broke my arm; the second time, he pierced my lung; and the third time, he gave me this wound.” The Englishman turned down a collar that was up to his ears and showed a scar whose redness indicated it was relatively recent.
So I hold a deep grudge against him, the Englishman repeated, and he will surely die by my hand.
But, said the envoy from the prefecture, it seems to me that you are not on the path to kill him.
That was what the visitor wanted to know, or rather, it was all that the Englishman seemed to know.
The agent then stood up, and after greeting Lord Wilmore, who responded with the stiffness and politeness typical of the English, he withdrew.

For his part, Lord Wilmore, after hearing the street door close behind him, returned to his bedroom, where, in the blink of an eye, he lost his blond hair, his red sideburns, his false jaw, and his scar to regain the black hair, dark complexion, and pearl-like teeth of the Count of Monte Cristo.
The king's prosecutor was somewhat reassured by this double visit, which, in any case, had not taught him anything comforting, but also had not taught him anything alarming.
As a result, for the first time since the dinner at Auteuil, he slept the following night with some peace of mind.
They had reached the hottest days of July when this Saturday, when Mr. de Morcerf's ball was to take place, finally arrived in due course.

You two really had the meter, you pigs." Then Mathieu got angry: "Don't say that, Mélie, don't say that, I've never been to the meter." They served us an exquisite lunch, in front of the door, under two linden trees, next to the small chapel of "Our Lady of the Big Belly" and facing the vast landscape.
And Mathieu told us, with a teasing tone mixed with unexpected credulity, incredible stories of miracles.

We had drunk a lot of that lovely, tangy, sweet, fresh, and intoxicating cider that he preferred to all other drinks; and we were smoking our pipes, perched on our chairs, when two old women showed up.
They were old, thin, and bent.
After greeting us, they asked for Saint Blanc.
Mathieu winked at us and replied: He stayed there for a good five minutes; then he came back with a dismayed look.
He raised his arms:
"I don't know where he is, I can't find him; I'm sure I had him though."
Then, making a megaphone with his hands, he bellowed again: "Mélie-e-e!" From the back of the yard, his wife replied:

Isn't that the one you took last week to plug the hole in the rabbit hutch? Indeed, Saint Blanc, stuck in the ground like a simple stake, covered in mud and filth, served as a corner for the rabbit hutch.
He went to get some straw and made them a prayer stool.

Then, considering his filthy saint and, no doubt fearing a loss of reputation for his business, he added: He took a bucket of water, a brush, and began to wash the wooden figure vigorously while the two old women continued to pray.
Then, when he had finished, he added: 'Now there's no more harm.' And he brought us back to have a drink.
As he was bringing the glass to his mouth, he stopped and, looking a bit embarrassed, said: 'Still, when I put Saint Blanc with the rabbits, I really thought he wouldn't make any money.

But saints, you see, never go out of fashion.'

The baroness, pale and horrified, listened to this speech with as much dread and despair as Debray had shown calmness and indifference in delivering it.
"Abandoned!
she repeated, oh!
so abandoned...
Yes, you are right, sir, and no one will doubt my abandonment." These were the only words that this woman, so proud and so violently in love, could respond to Debray.
"But rich, very rich indeed," Debray continued, pulling out some papers from his wallet and spreading them on the table.
"Madam," said Debray, "it has been about six months since we became partners.
"It was in April of this year that our partnership was formed.
"In July, we added one hundred seventy thousand francs; that is, as you know, the month of Spanish bonds.

"In August, we lost three hundred thousand francs at the beginning of the month; but by the 15th we had recovered, and by the end we had taken our revenge; for our accounts, settled from the day of our partnership until yesterday when I closed them, show an asset of two million four hundred thousand francs, which means one hundred twenty thousand francs for each of us.
"Now," Debray continued, consulting his notebook with the method and calmness of a stockbroker, "we find eighty thousand francs for the compound interest on this sum that has remained in my hands.
--But, interrupted the baroness, what do these interests mean, since you have never put this money to use?
I beg your pardon, madam, said Debray coldly; I had your authority to act on your behalf, and I made use of your powers.
So that's forty thousand francs in interest for your share, plus the one hundred thousand francs of initial investment, which means three hundred and forty thousand francs for your portion.

Now, madam, Debray continued, I took the precaution of mobilizing your money the day before yesterday, not long ago, as you can see, and it would seem that I suspected I would soon be called to render my accounts to you.
Your money is there, half in banknotes, half in bearer bonds.

sentences: Indeed, the storm could be heard howling around the house.
The snow that was falling, already almost solidified, crackled against the frost on the windows.
High-pitched whistles, passing through the joints of the doors and windows, sometimes rose to the limit of audible sounds.
Then, a great silence fell.
Nature seemed to catch its breath, and once again, the gust unleashed itself with terrible force.
You could feel the house trembling on its stilts, the boards creaking, the beams groaning.
A stranger, less accustomed than the fort's inhabitants to these atmospheric convulsions, might have wondered if the storm would carry away this assembly of planks and beams.
But Captain Craventy's guests were little concerned about the gust, and even outside, they would not have been more frightened than those little birds that play in the midst of storms.
However, regarding these guests, a few observations need to be made.
The gathering included about a hundred individuals of both sexes; but only two

did not belong to the usual staff of Fort-Reliance.
This staff consisted of Captain Craventy, Lieutenant Jasper Hobson, Sergeant Long, Corporal Joliffe, and about sixty soldiers or employees of the Company.

Some of them were married, including Corporal Joliffe, a happy husband of a lively and alert Canadian woman, a certain Mac Nap, a Scot married to a Scottish woman, and John Raë, who had recently taken a wife from the local Indian women.

The nearby forts,

sentences: A great misfortune; but allow me to leave, it concerns something far more precious than my life.
No questions, count, I beg you, just a horse!
My stables are at your service, viscount, said Monte-Cristo; but you will exhaust yourself with fatigue by riding hard; take a carriage, a cab, any vehicle.

No, that would take too long, and besides, I need this fatigue that you fear for me, it will do me good." Albert took a few steps, spinning like a man struck by a bullet, and fell into a chair near the door.
Monte-Cristo did not see this second weakness; he was at the window shouting, "Ali, a horse for Mr.
de Morcerf!
Hurry up!
He is in a hurry!" These words revived Albert; he rushed out of the room, the count followed him.
"Thank you!"
murmured the young man as he jumped into the saddle.
You will return as quickly as you can, Florentin.
Is there a password so that they will give me horses?
Nothing but to return the one you are riding; another one will be saddled for you immediately." "You may find my departure strange, foolish, said the young man.

You do not understand how a few lines written in a newspaper can drive a man to despair; well, he added, throwing the newspaper at him, read this, but only after I have left, so you do not see my embarrassment." And while the count picked up the newspaper, he drove the spurs, which had just been fastened to his boots, into the horse's belly, which, astonished that there existed a rider who believed he needed such a stimulant, took off like a bolt from a crossbow.

The count followed the young man with an infinite sense of compassion, and it was only when he had completely disappeared that, turning his gaze back to the newspaper, he read the following: "He is now called Mr. Count de Morcerf, and is a member of the House of Peers."

Thus, this terrible secret, which Beauchamp had buried with such generosity, reappeared like an armed ghost, and another newspaper, cruelly informed, had published, the day after Albert's departure for Normandy, the few lines that had nearly driven the unfortunate young man mad.

sentences: During the first act, Countess G... entered her box;

her first glance was directed towards the spot where she had seen the Count the day before, so she caught sight of Franz and Albert in the box of the man about whom she had expressed such a strange opinion to Franz twenty-four hours earlier.

Her lorgnette was aimed at him with such intensity that Franz realized it would be cruel to delay any longer in satisfying her curiosity; thus, taking advantage of the privilege granted to spectators in Italian theaters, which allows them to treat the performance halls as their own reception rooms, the two friends left their box to pay their respects to the Countess.
Hardly had they entered her box when she signaled for Franz to take the place of honor.
"Well," she said, barely giving Franz time to sit down, "it seems you couldn't wait to get to know the new Lord Ruthwen, and now you are the best of friends?"
"Although we are not as far along in mutual intimacy as you suggest, I cannot deny, Madame Countess," replied Franz, "that we have taken advantage of his kindness all day long.

"Indeed, that's the word: this morning we accepted his invitation to lunch, during the entire masquerade we rode the Corso in his carriage, and finally, tonight we are attending the performance in his box.
"Alright, I like complete stories.
In the meantime, how did you come into contact?
Who introduced you to him?
"Well, we'll swallow that one along with the others," replied the Countess, who was from one of the oldest families in the vicinity of Venice; "and what kind of man is he, by the way?"

"We would be hard to please if we didn't find him charming, Madame," replied Albert; "a ten-year friend could not have done more for us than he has, and he did it all with a grace, delicacy, and courtesy that truly indicate a man of the world.

Come now, said the countess with a laugh, you'll see that my vampire will simply be some nouveau riche who wants to atone for his millions, and who will have adopted Lara's look so that he won't be confused with Mr. Rothschild.
